With many modern horror games either being "2DEEP4U" walking simulators or "Merry Monster Chase" action adventures, I would like to know what kind of creepy gameplay mechanics /v/gaming would like to see more often in Horror Games.

One thing I personally would find highly enjoyable would be a greater focus on sound, and, in particular, on EVPs. For those in the know, EVPs are "Electric Voice Phenomena", that is, supposed voice recordings of ghosts or other incorporeal creatures captured via microphones. The only horror game I can think of that actually makes EVPs one of the major elements in its gameplay is Silvio, and indie horror title with a fairly interesting concept, but rather lackluster execution.

Of course, this is just one potential example - what is stuff you would like to see more in horror games?
Gameplay Mechanics in Horror Games you would like to see more
No safe zones/no pausing. I loved it in Deadspace. The feeling that you can be attacked at any moment at any place, even if you go into your inventory or go into a shop, really helps sets the mood.

I don't really want to see anything in particular in horror games because I simply don't play them. I'd rather have a game all about gameplay, or one that doesn't try to either jumpscare me (that's a big no-no) or play with my emotions in some way. Basically only Undertale gets away with that last thing while not feeling forced.

That said, I think I have enough perspective to say this: a horror game with engaging gameplay needs to include something that the player wants to avoid (jumpscare being the obvious one), and to tie that bad consequence to bad choices that the player can make. Maybe the consequence is very gradual, but it needs to be there as a form of soft (or hard) failure to mesh gameplay into the theme. A game that manages to do this creates tension by tying the bad consequences to challenges that you can either fail or succeed, rather than giving you jumpscares for no reason or just making you do challenging things unrelated to the creepy environment.

One thing that I think Bioshock and Dead Space both did really well - higher difficulty means fewer resources, rather than enemies simply doing more damage and taking less.

The first 45 minutes of Resident Evil 4 is far more nerve-wracking than any other sections, simply because you actually need to worry about running out of ammunition and items. A lot of games do it.... In the beginning. But there are few games that manage to preserve that feel for their entire duration.

The "don't look at the monster" mechanic from Amnesia, where looking at the monster decreases your sanity. Firstly, is punishes you for looking at the monster which pretty much solidifies the golden rule of horror films (don't show the monster, what you don't see is more scary than what you do see) in to a gameplay mechanic. Secondly, by punishing looking at the monster, you make "peeking" to see if it's safe that much more terrifying, since there are actual gameplay ramifications for doing so.

Agreed, that mechanic really solidified Amnesia as a good horror game. If I remember correctly, the sequel removed that mechanic and with the story quality aside, the game really suffered from that. The pig monsters just really didn't terrify me like the monster in Amnesia.

Doesn't really answer your question but it is something i've been wanted for awhile now.

I really want a game where the first half is Alien: Isolation. You are hiding from an unknown monster in a large dark location (factory, mansion, cave system/forest, anywhere that fits the aesthetic you're wanting). The monster has free reign and so encounters will never be the same. But then half way through the game the roles are switched and you are hunting the monster as it hides from you. Both sides need great level design, lighting, and sound design.

PUZZLES!!

Okay, so not what you'd expect to hear, but you need some down time in horror games just to take a break between those tense moments. So when I say puzzles, I don't just mean get key into door, I mean get to get to door, and unlock it with mini-game puzzle (rotate between two dials, when symbols match door opens sort of thing) there just need to be puzzles.

No kill animal rescue is a disaster for animal welfare

Was looking at breeder websites one day and one woman said she wasn't breeding anymore due to the seedy rescue industry (to paraphrase). Made me curious and then I saw this today. I've heard a lot of stories about rescue animals having problems. This essay brings up a lot of good questions about the issue.
Legit no kill shelters tend to not allow adoptions and will immediately send you to the nearest kill shelter. Also there is the problem of rescues being fronts for puppy mills.

I tried to get a sheltie through a sheltie rescue and they were beyond rude. Said I wasn't fit to own a dog because I work a stable full time job. Let that one soak in a minute. So I went to a breeder. Single mom breeding in house, experienced and gave them amazing care, trying to go back to school. Did not feel one bit bad buying a dog from her!

To be honest, I probably would have told you the same thing and insisted you adopt two or none. The more intelligent the dog, the more psychologically damaging it is for them to be left alone for long periods of time and there are dogs that can't emotionally handle being alone for even shorts periods of time.

I don't know why you would. Most people who have dogs also work full time. Otherwise how can you afford them?

He goes to daycare. They never asked me what I intended to do with the dog all day. And he does agility. As he is getting older daycare everyday is a bit much. He's even been so tired that he'll choose to stay home some days (gets in his kennel and goes back to sleep). He's a good little dog. I keep him active and give him lots of love.

Realize that you aren't a whole lot of people like you. Most pet owners don't take the responsibility serious and have no consideration for the emotional needs of their pets. When I used to volunteer in animal rescue, the amount of animals there because they had neglect related behavior issues was significant and these abuses are often committed by well-meaning people. I'm glad you are a responsible owner but those that aren't are numerous.

It's true, there are a some bad people out there. There's also a lot of clueless ones. Like the woman in the story, we've all grown up relating to animals in different ways. I don't think there is one right way. What was right for my partner's hunting dogs is not going to be right for my sheltie. There's a lot of wrong ways out there too. There are still trainers that choke out dogs. I grew up with dogs that didn't get much exercise outside of the yard and hung out on the couch while my parents were at work or until we got home from school. Even with their highly intelligent standard poodle, they have never had problems with behavior and I definitely wouldn't say the dogs suffer. They get play and love, nothing like daycare (which can lead to behavior problems if it isn't a good place or doesn't fit the dog) or agility or going to dog parks. The important thing I think prospective owners need to know is that when behavior issues pop up there is a need not being met. Not all dogs are 9-5 couch potatoes and most need more stimulation and exercise. Still, there are 2 types of owner that make me cringe. People who keep large dogs in apartments and don't get them a lot of outdoor exercise and socialization, and people like my partner's ex who adopt dogs and get rid of them after 3-6 months (seriously, her name should be on a list somewhere banning her from adoption and buying from breeders).
